title: Bruschetta al Pomodoro
subtitle: Grilled bread with fresh tomato, garlic, and olive oil
excerpt: Bruschetta al pomodoro is grilled sourdough rubbed with raw garlic and topped with chopped ripe tomatoes, olive oil, and sea salt. It takes about 10 minutes and depends entirely on good tomatoes and good oil. Serve it immediately before the bread goes soft.
sourceNotes: Bruschetta is one of the oldest Italian bread preparations, with roots in central Italy (Umbria, Lazio, Abruzzo) where olive oil has been pressed for centuries. The word derives from the Romanesco dialect term 'bruscare', meaning to toast over coals. The tomato version is a modern variant; the original bruschetta was bread rubbed with oil and salt only.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Season the tomatoes and leave for up to 30 minutes for the salt to draw out their juice. Toast the bread just before serving.

content.text: Bruschetta al pomodoro is grilled bread, raw garlic, ripe tomatoes, and good olive oil. The bread soaks up the tomato juice the moment you top it, so it must be eaten immediately. This is a summer dish; it needs tomatoes that are fully ripe, not supermarket ones that are red but flavourless. With good tomatoes in July or August, it is one of the best things you can eat in under 10 minutes.
Roughly chop the tomatoes and season with salt. Leave for 10 to 15 minutes while the salt draws out the juice.
Toast the bread on a griddle pan or under a grill until golden on both sides with visible char lines.
While the bread is still hot, rub each slice firmly with the cut face of a garlic clove. The bread acts as a grater and the garlic melts into the surface.
Spoon the tomatoes over the bread, including the juice. Drizzle generously with olive oil. Add basil if using and eat immediately.

Bruschetta in its simplest form is bread rubbed with olive oil and toasted over a fire. It has been made this way in central Italy since olive oil was first pressed in the region. The tomato version came later, after tomatoes became a staple in Italian cooking in the 18th and 19th centuries. Today the tomato bruschetta is so common that many people think it is the original; it is not, but it is the most popular.
